en.title: Land Grants and Changing Agrarian Society
en.summary: Land grants are among the most informative written records for the social and economic history of early medieval eastern India, but they are also among the easiest to overread. A copper-plate charter can describe a village, its boundaries and resources, the dues attached to it, the exemptions granted to a beneficiary, the officials and residents who were notified, and the religious or scholarly purpose of the donation.

mai.title: भूमिदान आ बदलैत कृषक समाज
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “भूमिदान आ बदलैत कृषक समाज” विषयक भूमि, गाम-नगर, पेशा, सामाजिक वर्गीकरण, पञ्जी, विवाह, राज्य आ प्रवासनक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: The problem: land, rights and documentary evidence
Copper plates as durable legal instruments
The Nandapur antecedent in the Munger region
From sale-and-gift procedure to royal śāsana

en.title: Village, Market and Town
en.summary: Settlement history is the study of relationships among people, production, exchange, institutions and movement. Early medieval eastern India cannot be reduced either to a landscape of self-sufficient villages or to an unbroken survival of ancient cities. The evidence instead shows differentiated settlements connected by fiscal orders, markets, rivers, roads, courts and religious institutions.

mai.title: गाम, बजार आ नगर
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “गाम, बजार आ नगर” विषयक भूमि, गाम-नगर, पेशा, सामाजिक वर्गीकरण, पञ्जी, विवाह, राज्य आ प्रवासनक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Settlement categories as historical relationships
The vocabulary: grāma, haṭṭa, pura, nagara and caturaka
The village was not a self-sufficient cell
Villages in the Tīrabhukti charter landscape

en.title: Labour, Service and Occupational Communities
en.summary: Early medieval social history is often reconstructed from landholders, rulers and institutions because they dominate the written record. This chapter reverses the angle of vision. It asks who cultivated fields, carried messages, guarded roads, supervised ferries, made tools, carved images, copied documents, supplied monasteries and performed the countless services that turned rights on copper plates into functioning society. The evidence does not permit a complete occupational census.

mai.title: श्रम, सेवा आ पेशागत समुदाय
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “श्रम, सेवा आ पेशागत समुदाय” विषयक भूमि, गाम-नगर, पेशा, सामाजिक वर्गीकरण, पञ्जी, विवाह, राज्य आ प्रवासनक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Labour as a historical problem
Occupation, service, status and caste are not synonyms
Four evidence streams and their limits
The Bhagalpur plate as a social document

en.title: Social Classification and Its Historical Formation
en.summary: Social hierarchy in early medieval Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga was real, but its categories were historical rather than timeless. Land, office, ritual authority, occupation, migration, household standing and stigma generated overlapping distinctions. This chapter reconstructs how those distinctions became socially legible and, in some settings, increasingly hereditary.

mai.title: सामाजिक वर्गीकरण आ ओकर ऐतिहासिक निर्माण
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “सामाजिक वर्गीकरण आ ओकर ऐतिहासिक निर्माण” विषयक भूमि, गाम-नगर, पेशा, सामाजिक वर्गीकरण, पञ्जी, विवाह, राज्य आ प्रवासनक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Social classification as a historical problem
Varṇa and jāti must be kept analytically distinct
Four evidence streams and their limits
The Munger plate: classification in an administrative act

en.title: Brahmanical Institutions without Retrospective Caste Projection
en.summary: This chapter reconstructs Brahmanical institutions in medieval Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga through land grants, learned credentials, ritual and juristic expertise, household transmission, migration and patronage. Its governing method is chronological: early-medieval Brahman identities are described in the categories actually attested in their sources, while the later corporate organisation of Maithil Brahmans is reserved for the evidence that documents it.

mai.title: उत्तरकालीन जाति-प्रक्षेपण बिना ब्राह्मणिक संस्थान
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “उत्तरकालीन जाति-प्रक्षेपण बिना ब्राह्मणिक संस्थान” विषयक भूमि, गाम-नगर, पेशा, सामाजिक वर्गीकरण, पञ्जी, विवाह, राज्य आ प्रवासनक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Institution before caste category
What counts as a Brahmanical institution
Four evidence streams and a chronology firewall
Land grants as institutional documents

en.title: The Panji Tradition
en.summary: The Panji tradition transformed genealogy into an institution of social memory, territorial identity and marriage regulation in Mithila. This chapter treats the Panji neither as an timeless survival nor as a single document created once and thereafter unchanged.

mai.title: पञ्जी परम्परा
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “पञ्जी परम्परा” विषयक भूमि, गाम-नगर, पेशा, सामाजिक वर्गीकरण, पञ्जी, विवाह, राज्य आ प्रवासनक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Genealogy becomes an institution
What “Panji” means historically
Four evidence streams and a chronology firewall
Harisimhadeva and fourteenth-century formalisation

en.title: Women, Marriage and Property in Medieval Mithila
en.summary: Women’s social and economic history in medieval Mithila cannot be reconstructed by taking a single legal rule and treating it as a transparent description of life. The most articulate surviving materials are juristic: Sanskrit digests that classify marriage, gifts, inheritance, maintenance and household obligations. Those texts are indispensable because they preserve categories and arguments used by learned specialists, yet they are normative and selective.

mai.title: मध्यकालीन मिथिलामे महिला, विवाह आ सम्पत्ति
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “मध्यकालीन मिथिलामे महिला, विवाह आ सम्पत्ति” विषयक भूमि, गाम-नगर, पेशा, सामाजिक वर्गीकरण, पञ्जी, विवाह, राज्य आ प्रवासनक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Women’s history as a source problem
Normative rule is not observed practice
The chronological frame: Karnata, Oiniwar and later medieval Mithila
Mithila’s legal-digest tradition

en.title: Karnata and Oiniwar-Period Social Economy
en.summary: The Karnata and Oiniwar centuries are often narrated through rulers, invasions and genealogies, yet their historical significance also lies in the institutions that converted land, labour, knowledge and movement into durable social power. The Karnata kingdom, conventionally dated from Nanyadeva’s establishment of power in 1097 to the Tughluq conquest of 1324, was centred on Simraungadh and linked the middle Gangetic plain to the Himalayan foothills.

mai.title: कर्णाट आ ओइनिवार कालक सामाजिक अर्थव्यवस्था
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “कर्णाट आ ओइनिवार कालक सामाजिक अर्थव्यवस्था” विषयक भूमि, गाम-नगर, पेशा, सामाजिक वर्गीकरण, पञ्जी, विवाह, राज्य आ प्रवासनक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Two dynastic phases, not two sealed economies
The source base and its asymmetries
A Himalayan–Gangetic regional economy
Karnata state formation and Simraungadh

en.title: Islam, Migration and New Social Worlds
en.summary: Islam entered the social history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga through more than conquest. From the thirteenth century onward, the region stood inside a widening field of movement linking Delhi and the middle Ganga plain, Lakhnauti and Bengal, Jaunpur, Bihar, Anga and the routes toward Nepal. Armies and governors mattered, but so did merchants, transporters, scribes, scholars, Sufis, artisans, soldiers seeking employment, refugees and households that moved with patrons or opportunity.

mai.title: इस्लाम, प्रवासन आ नव सामाजिक संसार
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “इस्लाम, प्रवासन आ नव सामाजिक संसार” विषयक भूमि, गाम-नगर, पेशा, सामाजिक वर्गीकरण, पञ्जी, विवाह, राज्य आ प्रवासनक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Islam as a social history, not an invasion label
Source control: chronicles, inscriptions, literature and memory
Before 1324: a connected frontier already in formation
The 1324 Tughluq attack: political rupture, not demographic zero point

en.title: Persianate Culture and Mithila–Anga
en.summary: Persianate culture reached Mithila and Anga through administration, courts, Sufi networks, inscriptions, books, routes and material practices rather than through one uniform process. This chapter reconstructs that field without treating “Persianate” as an ethnic identity, without equating it with Islam as a whole, and without assuming that elite documentary change automatically transformed village speech or social life.

mai.summary: ई अध्याय “फारसीकृत संस्कृति आ मिथिला-अंग” विषयक भूमि, गाम-नगर, पेशा, सामाजिक वर्गीकरण, पञ्जी, विवाह, राज्य आ प्रवासनक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Defining “Persianate” without ethnic or religious conflation
Source control: what a cultural history can and cannot prove
Bihar inside the Persian cosmopolis
Persian as an administrative technology
